## Vicks VapoRub



What's been studied. One small pilot study, 18 people, applied the ointment daily to fungal toenails for 48 weeks. At the end, 5 of the 18 had a nail that was both clear and fungus-free on the lab test, 10 had partial improvement, and 3 had no change. The active ingredients thought to matter are camphor, menthol, and eucalyptus oil, which have antifungal activity in the lab.

What that means. A result worth knowing about: about a quarter cured in a tiny, uncontrolled study, with nobody comparing it to doing nothing. It's cheap and safe on intact skin. It's not a first choice, and for a man who can take the pill it's a poor trade against a treatment that cures nearly twice as many in a controlled trial. Reasonable as an add-on, or for a mild infection at the tip in a man who has decided against prescriptions.

## Tea tree oil

What's been studied. One trial from the 1990s compared 100% tea tree oil applied twice daily for six months with a 1% antifungal cream that isn't itself a nail treatment. Both groups improved by about the same amount on looks, and both did poorly on the lab test. A later trial of a tea tree cream combined with an antifungal drug showed some benefit, but the drug may have done the work.

What that means. Tea tree oil has antifungal activity in the lab and weak, old evidence on nails. It irritates skin in some people and can cause an allergic rash. If you use it, it's on the nail plate only, not the skin fold, and it's a supporting act.

## Snakeroot extract

What's been studied. A Mexican plant, Ageratina pichinchensis, in a couple of small trials against ciclopirox lacquer, with roughly similar results. Ciclopirox's own complete cure rate is under 1 in 10, so "similar to ciclopirox" is a low bar. Hard to find in a standardized form outside those trials.
chunks.section: Apple cider vinegar and other soaks

chunks.title: Home Remedies for Toenail Fungus: Vicks, Tea Tree, Laser
chunks.text:
Ciclopirox's own complete cure rate is under 1 in 10, so "similar to ciclopirox" is a low bar. Hard to find in a standardized form outside those trials.



## Apple cider vinegar and other soaks

What's been studied. Nothing on toenails. Apple cider vinegar is the usual version and plain white vinegar the cheaper one; the idea is that fungus dislikes acid, which is true in a dish. On a nail, a daily 15-minute soak in diluted vinegar doesn't reach the fungus under the plate, and a year of it hasn't been tested anywhere.

What that means. Harmless on intact skin, useless as a cure. The soak does soften the nail, which makes filing easier; if you like the ritual, file afterward and count that as the benefit. Bleach soaks, sometimes recommended online, damage skin and aren't worth the risk.

## Hydrogen peroxide

What's been studied. Nothing on toenails. Peroxide kills fungus on a surface, in a dish, and on the skin around a nail; it doesn't get through the plate, and a daily foot soak in it dries and irritates the skin, which is the opposite of what a foot fighting fungus needs.

What that means. Skip it. If you want a soak before filing, plain warm water does the useful part.

## Listerine (mouthwash)

What's been studied. Nothing on toenails. The logic is the alcohol, menthol, thymol, and eucalyptol in the original formula, which have activity against fungus in the lab. A daily foot soak in it reaches the skin and the nail surface, not the nail bed.

What that means. Harmless, and a cheap way to make the filing ritual happen; not a treatment. Some men mix it with vinegar, which is two non-treatments in one bowl.

## Baking soda, garlic, oregano oil, coconut oil, ozonated oils

What's been studied. Lab-dish activity for several of them, no nail trials for any.

What that means. Skip, or treat as harmless if it comes with filing and drying. Don't let any of them stand in for treatment past the first month.

## Drugstore "fungal nail" kits

chunks.title: Home Remedies for Toenail Fungus: Vicks, Tea Tree, Laser
chunks.text:
What that means. Skip, or treat as harmless if it comes with filing and drying. Don't let any of them stand in for treatment past the first month.

## Drugstore "fungal nail" kits



Most contain urea, which softens and thins the nail, or a cosmetic whitener, or a low-strength antifungal that penetrates nail poorly. Urea is useful: a thinner nail responds better to any real treatment, and a 40% urea cream at night for a few weeks does the job. The rest is packaging. Read the ingredients; if the active ingredient isn't a named antifungal drug at a nail-treatment concentration, it isn't a nail treatment.

## Laser

What's been studied. More than the home remedies, and the picture is still poor. The devices heat the nail to damage the fungus. The regulatory clearance is for a "temporary increase in clear nail", which is a cosmetic claim. The most careful review of the trials found them small, short, and inconsistent, with low certainty of any benefit, and clearance rates well below oral treatment. A few better-run studies show some improvement when laser is combined with a topical, but the topical may be doing the work.

The cost. Several hundred to over a thousand dollars for a course, almost never covered by insurance.

What that means. If you can't take the pill and the topical alone has failed, laser plus topical is a defensible thing to try with a podiatrist who is honest about the odds. On its own, for the price, it's the worst value on this page.

## What all of this shares

Every remedy above works better in the stories than in the studies for the same reasons: the nail gets filed, cleaned, and trimmed as part of the ritual, which improves the look; the skin dries out because someone is paying attention; and in half the cases there was no fungus to begin with. Those are real benefits. They're just not the remedy.

If you want to use a home remedy, do it like this:

chunks.title: Home Remedies for Toenail Fungus: Vicks, Tea Tree, Laser
chunks.text:
Those are real benefits. They're just not the remedy.

If you want to use a home remedy, do it like this:



1. Diagnosis first. A nail clipping test at the podiatrist.
2. Alongside, not instead. Prescription treatment does the killing; the remedy is company.
3. Filing and drying every time. That's the part that helps.
4. Photos monthly. If the clear band at the base isn't growing by month three, the remedy isn't working, and the 12-month protocol explains what should be.
5. Stop at the first sign of skin irritation. Redness or blistering around the nail means the remedy is doing harm.

## Bottom line

Vicks has one small, promising, uncontrolled study. Tea tree oil has old, weak evidence and a rash risk. Snakeroot matches a weak prescription. Vinegar, baking soda, garlic, mouthwash, and peroxide have no nail evidence at all. Urea thins the nail and helps real treatment; that's the one drugstore ingredient worth buying. Laser is expensive and unproven on its own. Get the diagnosis, take the treatment with the best odds, and keep any remedy in the supporting role. Choosing that treatment starts at treatments, compared.

chunks.title: Toenail Fungus Treatments Compared: Pills, Topicals, Laser
chunks.text:
# Toenail Fungus Treatments, Compared: Pills, Topicals, Laser, and What Cures

There are five ways to treat toenail fungus, and they don't work equally. The difference between the best and the worst is not a few percentage points; it's the difference between a nail that clears in most men and one that clears in fewer than one in ten. Most men never see those numbers because the products are sold on hope, not results.

This guide puts the options side by side: what each one is, how well it works in trials, what it costs, and who it suits. It assumes the diagnosis is confirmed. If it isn't, start with is it toenail fungus?, because none of this helps a nail that was never infected. Toenail fungus: what works has the one-page ranking if you want the short version first.

One word on "cure". Trials measure two things: the fungus gone from the lab test (mycological cure) and the nail fully normal to look at (complete cure). Complete cure is the number that matters to you and it's always the lower one. The figures below are complete cure unless stated.

## The pill: terbinafine

What it is. A tablet, taken once a day for 12 weeks for toenails. It travels through the blood into the nail bed and keeps working there for months after the last dose, which is why a 3-month course treats a 12-month problem.

How well it works. The best of the lot. In the trials that got it approved, about 4 men in 10 reached a completely normal nail and about 7 in 10 were fungus-free on the lab test. Real-world numbers are a little lower, and the odds fall with age, with how much of the nail is involved, and with slow circulation.

chunks.title: Toenail Fungus Treatments Compared: Pills, Topicals, Laser
chunks.text:
Real-world numbers are a little lower, and the odds fall with age, with how much of the nail is involved, and with slow circulation.



What to know before you take it. It's a generic and cheap. It's processed by the liver, so doctors check a liver blood test before starting and sometimes during; serious liver harm is rare but real, and anyone with liver disease is steered elsewhere. Some men notice a change in taste or smell, which usually resolves after the course but occasionally lingers. It interacts with a few medications, including some antidepressants and heart drugs, so bring your full list. It doesn't have the cholesterol-drug interaction that the other pill has.

Who it suits. Most men over 40 with a confirmed infection that involves more than the tip of the nail, more than a couple of nails, or the nail's base. Also anyone who has already failed a year of topical treatment.

## The other pill: itraconazole

What it is. A capsule, taken daily for 12 weeks or in one-week "pulses" each month for three months.

How well it works. Clearly less than terbinafine: roughly 1 man in 7 reaches a completely normal nail. It's the pill for cases where terbinafine can't be used or the lab finds a yeast or mold rather than a dermatophyte.

What to know. This one has the interaction problem. It blocks the enzyme that clears many common drugs, and some cholesterol medications (simvastatin and lovastatin in particular) can't be taken with it at all. It also carries a warning for men with heart failure. For a man over 40 on a statin, that alone usually settles the choice.

## Prescription topicals

Three prescription liquids or lacquers, painted on the nail daily for 48 weeks. They avoid the liver entirely and suit mild infections: the tip of the nail, less than about half its area, the base not involved, and no more than three or four nails.

chunks.title: Toenail Fungus Treatments Compared: Pills, Topicals, Laser
chunks.text:
They avoid the liver entirely and suit mild infections: the tip of the nail, less than about half its area, the base not involved, and no more than three or four nails.



Efinaconazole solution (Jublia). The best of the topicals. About 1 man in 6 reached a completely normal nail after a year in its trials, and about half were fungus-free on the lab test. It penetrates the nail better than the older lacquers and doesn't need filing. It's expensive without insurance.

Tavaborole solution (Kerydin). Similar idea, slightly weaker results: well under 1 in 10 complete cure in its trials.

Ciclopirox lacquer (Penlac). The old one and the cheap one; a generic exists. Applied daily, removed with alcohol once a week, with the nail trimmed and filed monthly. Complete cure is low, around 1 in 12 to 1 in 18, and it's a full year of daily discipline for that.

How to raise the odds with any topical. File the nail thin first, and keep it thin; a podiatrist can grind it down properly in minutes. Treat the skin between the toes at the same time. And apply every day; the failures in the trials are mostly people who stopped.

## Does Lamisil cream work on toenail fungus? The drugstore shelf

No. Lamisil AT and the other athlete's foot creams are terbinafine or a cousin of it, and they work on skin because skin is where they can reach; a nail plate stops them. They're the right thing for the peeling between your toes and the wrong thing for the nail. The rest of the over-the-counter "fungal nail" shelf is mostly urea, which softens the nail for filing, or a whitener; none has cure evidence, and home remedies and laser goes through it product type by product type.

## Laser

chunks.title: Toenail Fungus Treatments Compared: Pills, Topicals, Laser
chunks.text:
## Laser



A clinic treatment that heats the nail to damage the fungus, sold for several hundred to over a thousand dollars and rarely covered by insurance. Its clearance is for a "temporary increase in clear nail", a cosmetic claim, and the best review of the trials found small, inconsistent studies with clearance rates well below the pill; home remedies and laser has the evidence in full and the one case where laser plus a topical is worth trying.

## Thinning the nail: the step everyone skips

A podiatrist can file or grind a thick nail down to a thin plate in one visit, and a 40% urea cream at home does a slower version over weeks. It's not a cure on its own. It matters because every other treatment works better on a thin nail: less material for the fungus, less pressure in the shoe, and far better penetration for a topical. It's the cheapest improvement on this page.

## Combining treatments

Pill plus topical does better than either alone in several studies, particularly for stubborn cases, because they reach the fungus from two directions. Pill plus nail thinning is standard practice. Topical plus laser is what clinics offer men who can't take the pill. Ask the podiatrist which combination fits your nail; the answer depends on how much of it is involved and how long it has been there.

## Should the nail be removed?

chunks.title: Toenail Fungus Treatments Compared: Pills, Topicals, Laser
chunks.text:
Ask the podiatrist which combination fits your nail; the answer depends on how much of it is involved and how long it has been there.

## Should the nail be removed?



Sometimes, and rarely on its own. There are two ways to take a nail off: a chemical avulsion, where a high-strength urea paste under a dressing softens the nail over a week or two until it lifts away without cutting, and a surgical avulsion, done under local anesthetic in the office. Removing the nail doesn't cure the infection by itself, because the fungus is in the nail bed too and the new nail grows straight into it; studies of avulsion alone show poor cure rates. It earns its place for a nail so thick or painful that nothing can be applied to it, or paired with a topical painted on the exposed bed while the new nail grows. A permanent removal is a last resort for a man who has been through repeated courses and wants no more nail to infect. Ask about it if the nail hurts in every shoe; otherwise thinning does most of the same job with none of the downtime.

## Choosing

What each costs, roughly. Generic terbinafine is the cheapest by far: the 12-week course runs to a few tens of dollars at most pharmacies with a discount card, plus the blood test. Generic ciclopirox lacquer is tens of dollars a bottle, and a year takes several bottles. Efinaconazole (Jublia) and tavaborole (Kerydin) run to hundreds of dollars a bottle without insurance coverage, and a year usually takes more than one bottle. Laser is several hundred to over a thousand dollars for a course, almost never covered. Nail thinning by a podiatrist is an office visit. Cash prices move; check a discount-card price before you fill anything.

chunks.title: Toenail Fungus Treatments Compared: Pills, Topicals, Laser
chunks.text:
Nail thinning by a podiatrist is an office visit. Cash prices move; check a discount-card price before you fill anything.



- Confirmed, more than the tip, or several nails, no liver disease: terbinafine, with a liver test first and the topical on top if the podiatrist suggests it. Highest odds, lowest cost.
- Mild, a tip or an edge, one to three nails: a prescription topical for a year, nail kept thin, skin treated.
- Can't take the pill (liver disease, interactions, your choice): topical plus thinning, laser optional.
- On a statin: terbinafine is usually fine; itraconazole usually isn't. Confirm with the prescriber.
- Diabetes or poor circulation: the podiatrist decides, and sooner rather than later, because these nails cause more trouble.

Whatever you choose, the calendar is the same: 12 to 18 months for a big toenail to grow out clear. The 12-month protocol covers what to do in each of them.

## Bottom line

The pill cures the most, costs the least, and needs a blood test and a medication check first. The prescription topicals cure some mild cases with a year of daily use. Drugstore products and laser have no cure evidence worth the money. Nail thinning improves all of them. Get the diagnosis, bring your medication list, and pick the route with the podiatrist. Bring the doctor-prep checklist so the visit covers the liver test and the interactions.

# Toenail Fungus: What Works, What's a Scam, and Where to Start

Toenail fungus isn’t dangerous.  
It’s just stubborn.

Most advice promises fast fixes or miracle products, then delivers results that don’t line up with reality.

This page is the short version and the map. It ranks the five ways to treat toenail fungus by how often they produce a normal nail, names the ones that are a year lost, and points to the five guides that cover each step in depth: whether it's fungus at all, the treatments compared, the twelve months of treatment, keeping it from coming back, and what the home remedies have behind them.

## Start here

Pick the guide that matches where you are.

Not sure it's fungus. About half of thick, yellow nails aren't fungal, and a month of the wrong treatment proves nothing. Is it toenail fungus? has the self-check, the look-alikes (old trauma, age, psoriasis, and the dark streak that needs a dermatologist), and why a five-minute clipping test comes before anything you buy.

Confirmed, choosing a treatment. Treatments, compared puts the pill, the other pill, the prescription topicals, the drugstore shelf, laser, and nail thinning side by side, with cure rates, rough costs, and the liver test and statin interaction that decide the route.

Treating, and month three looks like month one. The 12-month protocol explains why that is normal, what to do in each quarter, and how to tell the fungus is dying by the clear band at the base of the nail.

Clear, and never again. Keeping toenail fungus from coming back covers the shoes, socks, showers, and household, and the twice-weekly topical many podiatrists keep going after a cure.

chunks.title: Toenail Fungus: What Works, What's a Scam, Where to Start
chunks.text:
Clear, and never again. Keeping toenail fungus from coming back covers the shoes, socks, showers, and household, and the twice-weekly topical many podiatrists keep going after a cure.



Tempted by Vicks, vinegar, tea tree oil, or a laser ad. Home remedies and laser goes through the shelf in order of evidence: one small study, one old trial, a lot of nothing, and the single drugstore ingredient worth buying.

## My Experience With Toenail Fungus

I dealt with toenail fungus myself.

No miracle product cleared it, and there was no turning point I could point to.

What worked was showing up: filing the nail, applying the treatment, keeping the shoes dry. Every day for months, even when nothing looked different.

## What works, ranked

The five routes, from the one that cures the most to the one that cures the least. The figures are complete cure, a nail fully normal to look at, from the trials that approved each treatment. The detail and the sources are in treatments, compared.

chunks.title: Toenail Fungus: What Works, What's a Scam, Where to Start
chunks.text:
The figures are complete cure, a nail fully normal to look at, from the trials that approved each treatment. The detail and the sources are in treatments, compared.



1. Oral terbinafine. A daily tablet for 12 weeks. About 4 men in 10 reach a completely normal nail and about 7 in 10 are fungus-free on the lab test. A cheap generic, with a liver blood test first and your medication list checked. The best odds by a distance.
2. Oral itraconazole. Roughly 1 man in 7 reaches a normal nail. The pill for men who can't take terbinafine, or whose lab test finds a yeast or mold. It interacts with several common drugs, including some statins.
3. Prescription topicals. Efinaconazole (Jublia), tavaborole (Kerydin), and ciclopirox (Penlac), painted on daily for 48 weeks. Between about 1 in 6 and 1 in 18 reach a normal nail. For mild infections at the tip, and for men who can't take the pill.
4. Nail thinning. Not a cure on its own. It makes every other route work better and costs an office visit or a tube of 40% urea cream.
5. Laser. Cleared for a "temporary increase in clear nail", which is a cosmetic claim. Small, inconsistent studies; several hundred to over a thousand dollars; almost never covered.

Pill plus topical does better than either alone in stubborn cases, and pill plus thinning is standard practice.

## What's a scam, or close to it

Anything promising results in days or weeks. A toenail grows about a millimeter a month. New, clean nail starts at the cuticle and takes a year to reach the tip. The damaged nail in front of it never repairs; it grows out and gets trimmed off. No product changes that calendar.

Athlete's foot cream on the nail. Terbinafine cream, Lamisil AT and the rest, is the right thing for the peeling between your toes and the wrong thing for the nail, because it doesn't get through the plate. Treat the skin with it. Treat the nail with something that reaches the nail.
